title: Chapter XXII

teacherSummary.text: Collins proposes to Charlotte, who accepts for security. Elizabeth is shocked that her friend could marry so foolish a man. Charlotte says she is 'not romantic.'

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being sly
vocabulary.context: But here, she did injustice to the fire and independence of his character, for it led him to escape out of Longbourn House the next morning with admirable slyness, and hasten to Lucas Lodge to throw himself at her feet.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “slyness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The whole family in short were properly overjoyed on the occasion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overjoy”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth took an opportunity of thanking her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “thank”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To ascertain or determine by mathematical processes, usually by the ordinary rules of arithmetic
vocabulary.context: Lady Lucas began directly to calculate with more interest than the matter had ever excited before, how many years longer Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “calculate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “But is there not danger of Lady Catherine’s disapprobation here, my good sir?—You had better neglect your relations, than run the risk of offending your patroness.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “offend”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A cheerful readiness, willingness, or promptitude
vocabulary.context: Sir William and Lady Lucas were speedily applied to for their consent; and it was bestowed with a most joyful alacrity.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “alacrity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bennet with great politeness and cordiality said how happy they should be to see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other engagements might allow him to visit them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cordiality”: cor- (Latin com-, "with") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To reduce to a lower position in one's own eyes, or in the eyes of others
vocabulary.context: Collins, was a most humiliating picture!—And to the pang of a friend disgracing herself and sunk in her esteem, was added the distressing conviction that it was impossible for that friend to be tolerably happy in the lot she had chosen.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “humiliate”: hum (Latin humus, "earth" / homo, "human") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of comparing two or more things together
vocabulary.context: Miss Lucas called soon after breakfast, and in a private conference with Elizabeth related the event of the day before.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conference”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The steady countenance which Miss Lucas had commanded in telling her story, gave way to a momentary confusion here on receiving so direct a reproach; though, as it was no more than she expected, she soon regained her composure, and calmly replied—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “regain”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXII,” how does Austen show a practical marriage? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXII develops the idea of a practical marriage. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXII to complicate the reader's understanding of a practical marriage. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a practical marriage responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a practical marriage. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: As he was to begin his journey too early on the morrow to see any of the family, the ceremony of leave-taking was performed when the ladies moved for the night; and Mrs. Bennet with great politeness and cordiality said how happy they should be to see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other engagements might allow him to visit them.

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is Charlotte's choice wise, sad, or both? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are slyness, overjoyed, thanking, calculate, offending. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “But here, she did injustice to the fire and independence of his character, for it led him to escape out of Longbourn House the next morning with admirable slyness, and hasten to Lucas Lodge to throw himself at her feet.” Webster's says: The quality or state of being sly. Now the word history: “slyness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “overjoy”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “thank”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. At 27, Charlotte had few prospects; marriage offered her home and status. Why does this chapter matter? Charlotte's choice offers a realistic counterpoint to romantic ideals. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a practical marriage.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: As he was to begin his journey too early on the morrow to see any of the family, the ceremony of leave-taking was performed when the ladies moved for the night; and Mrs. Bennet with great politeness and cordiality said how happy they should be to see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other engagements might allow him to visit them.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXII,” how does Austen show a practical marriage? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a practical marriage, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes a practical marriage. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
